questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

  

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2{y}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-(2{y}_{1})^{2}+3(2{y}_{1})({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2})-2({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =-4{y}_{1}^{2}+6{y}_{1}^{2}+12{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-2{y}_{1}^{2}-8{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

  

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2}+(-{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}+3{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{2})^{2}+4(-{y}_{2})({y}_{1}+3{y}_{2}) \\  & ={y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-12{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-11{y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{2} & =-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the first equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the second equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} & =-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{1})^{2}-6(-{y}_{1})(-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})+(-2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-12{y}_{1}^{2}+6{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+4{y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-7{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+5{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={x}_{1} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the first equation for ${x}_{1}$ and substituting it into the second equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={y}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+5{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{1}(-{y}_{1}-{y}_{2})-(-{y}_{1}-{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-5{y}_{1}^{2}-5{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-5{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

 

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =-{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for ${x}_{2}$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}-2({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})(-{y}_{2})-4(-{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-4{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 1 & -14\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ above. Find the matrix of the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $x=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2}]^{T}$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $y=[{y}_{1},{y}_{2}]^{T}$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
x=Py.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 9 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}19 & 9 \\ 9 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{2})(-{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})+2(-{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{2}{y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{1}^{2}+8{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+8{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{y}_{1}^{2}+9{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+10{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form Given a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ below. Find the matrix of the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066712/assets/8c8f1626eafc81b4700a0ddc015c210508d4db464970abc706831ea86659e8da.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $\mathbf{x}=[x_1, x_2]^T$ is a vector given by its coordinates in the standard basis and $\mathbf{y}=[ y_1, y_2 ]^T$ is the same vector but given in the coordinates relative to the basis that consists of the columns of $P,$ then 

$$
\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{y}.
$$

As a result, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & =({y}^{T}{P}^{T})\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}\,AP)\,y,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that the matrix of our form in the new basis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\,AP & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
